submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on a form of the verb 'be' (was, were, is, are, been, be, being; French est/ete) whose subject denotes an animate being: strongly for a person - a name, he/she/they, or a human noun ('the officer was' 11.0, 'the soldier was' 10.5, 'the suspect was' 9.8, 'the workers were' 9.2, 'the children were' 6.0) and more weakly for an animal ('the dog was' 5.4, 'the cat was' 5.3) - while an inanimate object, institution or abstraction as subject leaves it at baseline or in a weak middle band ('the report was' 0.0, 'the theory was' 0.0, 'the weather was' 0.0, 'it was' 0.0, 'there was' 0.0, 'the building was' 2.7, 'the company was' 5.2), and a non-'be' predicate about a person also leaves it at baseline ('the man went' 0.7, 'he said' 0.0, 'he had' 0.0, 'the suspect fled' 0.0). The same animacy response fires more weakly on animate nouns themselves, but only where the surrounding text already makes those people the topic of a statement - quantified or categorised groups ('229 patients' 10.4, '193 women', Wikipedia 'Category:People' / 'Category:Writers' lines 7-11) and objects of verbs like 'interviewed' ('the people' 8.8) - and not on inanimate nouns in the same frames ('229 samples' 2.7, 'Category:Films' 0.0, 'the samples' 0.8); its write direction promotes the forward-looking past participles (killed, arrested, injured, convicted, elected, appointed, diagnosed), and its opposite (positive) pole is weaker (scan max 8.8) and shares the be-form preference.
